source_text: Convertamur ad ipsas iam rationes recensendas per quas apostolus docet velari feminam oportere, an eaodem etiam virginibus competant, ut ex hoc quoque vocabuli communio inter virgines et non virgines constet, dum eaedem velaminis causae in utraque parte deprehenduntur. Si caput mulieris vir est, utique et virginis, de qua fit mulier illa quae nupsit, nisi si virgo tertium genus est monstruosum aliquod sui capitis. Si mulieri turpe est radi sive tonderi, utique et virgini. Proinde viderit saeculum aemulum dei, si ita virgini caesum capillum decori mentitur, quamadmodum et puero permissum. Ergo eui aeque non convenit radi sive tonderi, aeque convenit operiri. Si gloria viri est mulier, quanto magis virgo, quae et gloria sibi est? Si mulier ex viro et propter virum, costa illa Adae virgo primum fuit. Si mulier potestatem habere super caput debet, vel eo iustius virgo, ad quam pertinet quod in causa est. Si enim propter angelos, scilicet quos legimus a deo et caelo excidisse ob concupiscentiam feminarum, quis praesumere potest tales angelos maculata iam corpora et humanae libidinis reliquias desiderasse, ut non ad virgines potius exarserint, quarum flos etiam humanam libidinem excusat? Nam et scriptura sic suggerit: Et factum est, inquit, cum coepissent homines plures fieri super terram, et filiae natae sunt eis; conspicati autem filii dei filias hominum, quod pulchrae essent, acceperunt sibi uxores ex omnibus quas elegerunt. Hic enim nomen mulierum Graecum uxores sapit, quia de nuptiis mentio est. Cum ergo filias hominum dicit, manifeste virgines portendit, quae adhuc apud parentes deputarentur (nam nuptae maritorum nuncupantur), cum potuerit dixisse uxores hominum, aeque non adulteros nominans angelos, sed marites, dum innuptas sumunt filias hominum, quas natas supra dixit, sic quoque virgines significans. Supra natas, at hic angelis nuptas. Aliud eas nescio quam natas et dehinc nuptas. Debet ergo adumbrari facies tam periculosa, quae usque ad caelum scandala iaculata est, ut coram deo adsistens, cui rea est angelorum exterminatorum, ceteris quoque angelis erubescat, et malam illam aliquando libertatem capitis sui comprimat, iam nec hominum oculis offerendam. Sed etsi contaminatas iam feminas angeli illi appetissent, tanto magis propter angelos virgines velari debuissent, quanto magis propter virgines angeli deliquisse potuissent. Si autem et naturae praeiudicium adicit apostolus, quod honor sit mulieris redundantia capillorum, quia coma pro operimento est, utique hoc maxime virgini insigne est, quarum et ornatus ipse proprie sic est, ut concumulata in verticem ipsam capitis arcem ambitu crinium contegat.
thought_title: The Apostle's Reasons for Veiling Apply to Virgins
orientation: Tertullian is now reviewing the apostle Paul's arguments for why a woman must be veiled, to show that each reason applies equally to virgins.
pass_a_gloss: Let us turn now to reviewing the very reasons through which the apostle teaches that a woman ought to be veiled, whether the same reasons also apply to virgins, so that from this too the commonality of the word between virgins and non-virgins may be established, while the same causes of the veil are found in each group. If the head of the woman is the man, certainly also of the virgin, from whom that woman is made who has married, unless perhaps a virgin is some monstrous third kind with its own head. If it is shameful for a woman to be shaved or shorn, certainly also for a virgin. Accordingly, let the world that rivals God see to it, if it lies that cut hair is becoming to a virgin, just as it is also permitted to a boy. Therefore to her to whom it is equally not fitting to be shaved or shorn, it is equally fitting to be covered. If the woman is the glory of the man, how much more the virgin, who is also a glory to herself? If the woman is from the man and for the sake of the man, that rib of Adam was first a virgin. If the woman ought to have power over her head, by that much more justly the virgin, to whom belongs what is in question. For if it is because of the angels, namely those whom we read fell from God and from heaven because of desire for women, who can presume that such angels desired already defiled bodies and the remnants of human lust, so that they would not rather have burned for virgins, whose flower even excuses human lust? For Scripture also suggests thus: And it happened, it says, when men began to become many upon the earth, and daughters were born to them; but the sons of God, having seen the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, took for themselves wives from all whom they chose. For here the Greek name of women savors of wives, because there is mention of marriages. Therefore when it says daughters of men, it clearly points to virgins, who were still counted as being with their parents (for married women are called by the name of their husbands), when it could have said wives of men, equally not naming the angels adulterers, but husbands, while they take unmarried daughters of men, whom it said above were born, thus also signifying virgins. Above born, but here married to angels. I know them as nothing other than born and then married. Therefore so dangerous a face ought to be shadowed, which has hurled stumbling blocks even up to heaven, so that standing before God, to whom it is guilty of the exterminated angels, it may also blush before the other angels, and may suppress that evil liberty of its head, no longer to be offered even to the eyes of men. But even if those angels had desired already defiled women, by so much more ought virgins to have been veiled because of the angels, by how much more the angels could have fallen because of virgins. But if the apostle also adds the prejudgment of nature, that the honor of a woman is the abundance of hair, because the hair is for a covering, certainly this is especially the mark of virgins, whose very adornment is properly such, that piled up on the top it covers the very citadel of the head with a circuit of hair.

lemmas.gloss: to be shorn, to have hair cut
to be shadowed, to be veiled

choices.english: that a woman ought to be veiled
choices.why: Keeps the impersonal obligation of oportere and the passive infinitive, matching the apostle's teaching as a rule.
rejected: that women must wear a veil
that the female should cover her head

choices.term: tertium genus est monstruosum aliquod sui capitis
choices.english: is some monstrous third kind with its own head
choices.why: Preserves the sarcastic tone and the phrase sui capitis, which Tertullian uses to mock the idea of a virgin outside the man-woman order.
rejected: is some third species with a head of its own

choices.why: Aemulus means rival or envious; rendering as 'that rivals God' keeps the adversarial relation to God explicit.
rejected: the world that is God's enemy

choices.english: whose flower even excuses human lust
choices.why: Flos means the bloom or flower of virginity; 'excuses' keeps the legal-rhetorical sense that virgin beauty makes human desire understandable.
rejected: whose blossom even pardons human desire
whose flower even justifies human lust

choices.why: Sapit literally means 'tastes of'; keeping 'savors' preserves the metaphor that the Greek word for women here has the flavor or implication of wives.

choices.english: so dangerous a face ought to be shadowed
choices.why: Adumbro means to shade or veil; 'shadowed' keeps the visual metaphor of covering a dangerous face, and the passive infinitive preserves the obligation.
rejected: so dangerous a face must be covered
such a perilous countenance should be veiled

bible_refs.note: Et factum est, cum coepissent homines plures fieri super terram, et filiae natae sunt eis; conspicati autem filii dei filias hominum, quod pulchrae essent, acceperunt sibi uxores ex omnibus quas elegerunt.

pass_b_english: Let us now turn to the reasons the apostle gives for teaching that a woman ought to be veiled, and ask whether those same reasons apply to virgins as well. If they do, then the shared meaning of the word between virgins and non-virgins is established, since the same causes for the veil are found in both groups.
If the head of the woman is the man, then certainly the head of the virgin is the man too, for the married woman is made from a virgin. Unless a virgin is some monstrous third kind with its own head.

If it is shameful for a woman to be shaved or shorn, then certainly it is shameful for a virgin as well. Let the world that rivals God see to it, then, if it falsely claims that cut hair is becoming to a virgin, just as it has also permitted it for a boy. Therefore the one for whom it is equally unfitting to be shaved or shorn is equally fitting to be covered.
If the woman is the glory of the man, how much more the virgin, who is also a glory to herself? If the woman is from the man and for the sake of the man, that rib of Adam was first a virgin.
If the woman ought to have power over her head, then by even greater right the virgin ought to have it, for what is at issue belongs to her.

For if it is because of the angels—those whom we read fell from God and from heaven because of desire for women—who can presume that such angels desired bodies already defiled and the remnants of human lust, rather than that they burned more for virgins, whose flower even excuses human lust?

For Scripture also suggests this: "And it happened," it says, "when human beings began to multiply on the earth, and daughters were born to them, the sons of God saw the daughters of human beings, that they were beautiful, and took wives for themselves from all whom they chose" (Genesis 6:1-2).

Here the Greek word for women implies wives, because the mention is of marriage. So when it says "daughters of human beings," it clearly points to virgins, who would still be counted as belonging to their parents—for married women are called by their husbands' names—since it could have said "wives of human beings." Likewise it does not call the angels adulterers but husbands, while they take as wives the daughters of human beings, whom it said above were born, thus also indicating virgins. Above, born; here, married to angels. I know them as nothing other than born and then married.

So dangerous a face ought to be shadowed, a face that has hurled scandals all the way to heaven, so that as she stands before God, to whom she is answerable for the angels who were driven out, she may also blush before the other angels, and may restrain that evil liberty of her head, no longer to be offered even to the eyes of men.
But even if those angels had desired women already defiled, virgins ought all the more to be veiled because of the angels, inasmuch as the angels could have sinned all the more because of virgins.

And if the apostle adds also the judgment of nature, that a woman's honor is the abundance of her hair, because the hair is given as a covering, then certainly this is especially the mark of virgins, whose very adornment is properly such that, piled up on the crown, it covers the very citadel of the head with a circling mass of hair.

problems.quote: to whom she is guilty for the angels who were driven out
problems.why: 'rea est' means 'she is answerable/liable'; the English 'to whom she is guilty' confuses the reference — she is liable to God for the banished angels.
problems.fix: to whom she is answerable for the angels who were driven out
problems.ruling: Latin "cui rea est angelorum exterminatorum" = "to whom she is guilty of the exterminators of angels"; English "for the angels who were driven out" misreads "exterminatorum" as angels, altering meaning.

edits.old: to whom she is guilty for the angels who were driven out
edits.new: to whom she is answerable for the angels who were driven out

fixed: Changed 'to whom she is guilty' to 'to whom she is answerable': source 'cui rea est angelorum exterminatorum' means she is liable/answerable to God for the banished angels, not guilty to them.

problems.quote: the Greek word for women savors of wives
problems.why: 'Savors of' is archaic; likely means 'carries the connotation of' or 'implies.'
problems.fix: Render as 'the Greek word for women carries the sense of wives.'

edits.old: the Greek word for women savors of wives
edits.new: the Greek word for women carries the sense of wives

fixed: Changed 'savors of' to 'carries the sense of' because the source 'nomen mulierum Graecum uxores sapit' means the Greek term for women implies or connotes wives; 'savors of' is archaic and unclear.

polish.changed: Clarified pronoun references and speaker transitions, modernized archaic phrasing such as 'savors of,' broke long sentences into natural modern rhythm, and made the logical connections between the apostle's reasons and their application to virgins easier to follow aloud.

notes.quote: the Greek word for women savors of wives
notes.why: 'Savors of' is archaic; likely means 'carries the connotation of' or 'implies.'
notes.fix: Render as 'the Greek word for women carries the sense of wives.'

last_rejected.quote: Here the Greek word for women savors of wives, because the mention is of marriage.
last_rejected.source_quote: Hic enim nomen mulierum Graecum uxores sapit, quia de nuptiis mentio est.
last_rejected.why: “savors” is not in the Latin; the phrase means “means/signifies”.
last_rejected.fix: Here the Greek word for women, uxores, means “wives”, because the passage mentions marriage.
last_rejected.ruling: 'sapit' literally means 'tastes of/savors'; figurative use for 'has the flavor of' is standard Latin and within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: If the woman ought to have power over her head, then by even greater right the virgin ought to have it, for what is at issue belongs to her.
last_rejected.source_quote: Si mulier potestatem habere super caput debet, vel eo iustius virgo, ad quam pertinet quod in causa est.
last_rejected.why: Potestas super caput is the sign of authority worn upon the head (the veil), one of the apostle's reasons for veiling, not dominion over the head.
last_rejected.fix: If the woman ought to have authority upon her head, then by even greater right the virgin, since what is at issue pertains to her.
last_rejected.ruling: "potestatem habere super caput" rendered "power over her head" is literal; the translation keeps the ambiguity of 1 Cor 11:10 and the 'sign of authority' reading is interpretive.
